A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Conformal Prediction for Hierarchical Data. All 14 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, algorithms, and graphical results, are available and readable.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 2–3 report original synthetic experiments comparing five methods across 1,000 simulations.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report synthetic experiments and original evaluations on Palo Alto electric-vehicle charging data, including 360 repeated data splits.

M1.justification: The main componentwise algorithms retain their signed-residual, projection, and covariance-estimation procedures. As printed, the supplementary joint-region formula changes from a squared A-norm around the reconciled forecast in v1 Equation (41) to an unsquared A-norm around the base forecast in v2 Algorithm 5, line 7. The latter centering conflicts with v2's projected-score construction.

E1.justification: v2 adds daily charging-demand evaluation using 1,780 observations for five charging points in two Palo Alto stations. v1 evaluates only synthetic data. The retained synthetic hierarchy is the same 5–2–1 structure despite changes in level terminology.

E2.justification: Direct, OLS, WLS, Combi, and MinT remain the practical comparison methods. Oracle MinT, discussed theoretically in v1, is newly evaluated in v2's real-data comparison, as confirmed by Table 1 and Figures 2 and 8.

E3.justification: For the retained 100,000-sample simulations, reported feature generation changes from uniform to Gaussian, splits change from 4/7–1/7–1/7–1/7 to 40%–20%–20%–20%, and third-feature hiding changes from probability 0.7 to 0.3. v2 also introduces real-data random-split evaluation and an oracle that estimates covariance using calibration and test data. These establish reported protocol revisions, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix F.2 adds Student-density fits and Q-Q plots for two nodes (Figures 5–6), plus a comparison of practical and oracle covariance estimates for one run (Figure 7). These targeted diagnostics have no counterpart in v1, but remain limited to selected real-data examples.

E5.justification: v1 reports empirical averages and boxplots across 1,000 simulations. v2 adds explicitly defined 95% Monte Carlo confidence intervals for coverage and componentwise and total interval sizes, including transformed bounds for root-mean-square lengths. The synthetic run count remains 1,000; the real-data study reports 360 runs.

E6.justification: The synthetic plots change: WLS has smaller reported total lengths than Combi in v1 Figure 3, whereas Combi ranks ahead in v2 Figure 4. These results use revised settings. New real-data results show coverage near 90.5%, smaller total-length estimates for WLS and Combi than practical MinT, and the smallest estimate for Oracle MinT (Figure 8). These are new or replaced results, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 reformulates the basic efficiency theorem using elliptical scatter matrices without v1's global finite-covariance requirement. Appendices A–C add coverage bounds and tie/boundary-case arguments, broaden trace inequalities to positive-semidefinite settings, and replace the Lagrangian MinT proof with a direct decomposition proof. Componentwise oracle optimality itself was already established in v1 Theorem 4.2.

C1.justification: The central claims of combining SCP with reconciliation, preserving marginal coverage, reducing weighted interval sizes, and obtaining componentwise oracle optimality remain. v2 additionally identifies a trace inequality as its own contribution and presents the new elementary MinT proof as a contribution of independent interest.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking real-data overcoverage to finite calibration size and poor practical MinT performance to covariance-estimation difficulties. It acknowledges imperfect Student fits and explains the oracle's use of calibration/test data. v1 already discussed the general risk of inaccurate covariance estimation, so that limitation is expanded rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: Appendix F substantially expands reproducibility information beyond v1's brief Appendix B: random matrix and function-generation details, mgcv implementation, spline choices and degrees of freedom, and real-data selection and autoregressive features. It also specifies exactly how the practical and oracle covariance estimates are constructed.

R1.justification: v2 distinguishes its hierarchy from the settings of Lee, Dunn, and Duchi, adds references including Johnstone–Cox and Hyndman et al. (2016), and removes references including Jeon et al. (2019) and Brégère–Huard. Attribution of the trace contributions becomes more explicit, while the overall positioning as combining SCP and forecast reconciliation remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and much of the exposition are rewritten. The main text is reorganized around objectives, methodology, theoretical guarantees, and experiments; background and proofs are redistributed across Appendices A–F. v2 adds an appendix roadmap and removes the standalone conclusion.

P2.justification: v1's componentwise plot and total-length boxplot are redesigned and combined with real-data panels in v2 Figure 2; boxplots become estimates with confidence intervals. v2 adds the method-summary Table 1, Algorithms 4–5, and diagnostic Figures 5–7. Figures 4 and 8 enlarge results already displayed in Figure 2.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's simulation-only validation through real-data results, explicit uncertainty estimates, and detailed experimental documentation. The unfavorable practical MinT results help establish applicability limits, while expanded proofs clarify the theoretical framework. These gains outweigh the remaining joint-region inconsistency in Algorithm 5; the disclosed calibration/test-based oracle should still be interpreted only as an illustrative comparison.
